fields.title: Vetka: Four Ideas and One Quarter
fields.summary: Everyone proposed their own idea, and all sound reasonable. Decide how to test them so that in a quarter you actually know something for sure.
fields.decisionPrompt: How will you structure testing ideas this quarter?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager at Vetka.
fields.brief/company: Vetka is a subscription book-reading app. 400 thousand monthly active users, subscription starts after a seven-day free trial.
fields.brief/context: The goal for the quarter is to increase subscription conversion. Four ideas came up in the meeting. The tech lead suggests launching all four at once as an A/B test and 'seeing what wins'. The team stopped the previous experiment on day three because the difference looked convincing, and the rolled-out option had to be reverted later.
fields.brief/objective: At the end of the quarter, know not just 'what won', but why, so that future decisions are more accurate.
fields.brief/constraints: One part-time analyst, one developer dedicated to experiments. Organic traffic is about 11 thousand new users per week.
fields.brief/task: Decide how you will structure testing this quarter and explain why.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: One reliable answer is worth more than four noisy ones
fields.learnTakeaway/body: The temptation to test everything at once hits simple arithmetic: the more variants you have, the less data each gets, and the larger the effect must be to even be noticed. Usually, the right move is to expand the idea list cheaply, filter it down by reasoning, and use an experiment to test a single hypothesis so you can trust the result. And before the first serious test, make sure the measurement system isn't lying: that takes an hour.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Shorten the trial period from 7 days to 3 — proposed by the tech lead, brought up first, discussed the longest.

Show the subscription offer after the first chapter instead of at the end of the trial — proposed by the analyst.

Give the first book in full with no time limit — proposed by the designer, called naive in the meeting.

Remove registration before the first page — came from support, wasn't discussed.

The meeting was verbal only, no written phase. Out of six ideas voiced, four came from the two most senior participants.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Subscription conversion: 4.1%.
New organic users: about 11,000 per week. Paid traffic is counted separately — conversion there is 1.8% and user intent is different.

The analyst calculated: to reliably detect a 0.9 percentage point increase, you need about 22,000 people per variant — that is four weeks on two variants.

With four variants simultaneously, reaching that volume takes twelve weeks — the entire quarter — assuming the variants don't overlap.

An A/A test has never been run on this system. Event tracking was updated a month ago.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Tested a new payment screen. On day three, variant B was ahead by 12%, so they decided not to wait and rolled it out.

A month later, conversion reverted to the previous level. On post-mortem, they realized: during the first few days, weekend users were overrepresented in variant B — they read more and pay more often.

Before launch, neither duration, nor sample size, nor actions for ambiguous results were documented.

The post-mortem takeaway: 'wait until the end next time'. This never made it into a checklist or template.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
From the developer:

'Shortening the trial period is a config fix, half a day.
Showing the offer after the first chapter — three days.
First book in full with no time limit — one week, touches billing.
Removing registration before the first page — three weeks, refactoring auth.

Separately: a clickable prototype for any of these scenarios takes the designer one day to build. Five prototype interviews — another day.

Also: 6% of our users use offline mode, and we've been arguing for six months whether to keep developing it. Turning it off for 2% for two weeks — one hour of work.'
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Formulate hypotheses and test one properly
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Expand the list of ideas by varying parameters, turn the best into hypotheses with clear mechanisms, filter by cost of inaction, test the cheapest option with a prototype, and run a single 2-variant A/B test with a hypothesis card and a prior A/A test.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Varying the trial parameters yields several more options, including the one called naive at the meeting — first book with no time limit.
The A/A test finds a 1.4% discrepancy between identical variants: tracking from the previous update was counting an event twice. Fixed in a day. Without this, any result this quarter would be invalid.
You run a single experiment — offer after chapter one versus end of trial — for four weeks, with pre-defined outcomes. Result: 5.2% vs 4.1%.
The mechanism is verified separately: median time to subscription is 40 minutes, meaning the gain came from timing, not trial duration. This invalidates two of the four original ideas and sparks the next hypothesis.
Trade-off: only one hypothesis out of four was tested during the quarter, and the tech lead thought it was slow for two weeks.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Four ideas, one quarter. Split traffic into four variants and see which one wins.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Variants take twelve weeks to collect enough volume — the entire quarter, with no buffer.
In week six, one variant leads, and someone suggests not waiting again. This time you wait.
By the end of the quarter, only the largest effect is distinguishable; three variants out of four end up within noise, and what to do with them is unclear — it wasn't discussed in advance.
On top of that, the 'remove registration' option was never launched: it required three weeks of dev work that nobody scheduled.
Trade-off: you spent the whole quarter and got one weak takeaway instead of one reliable insight.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Take the trial shortening idea and ship it
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: It was discussed the longest and takes half a day to fix. Roll it out to everyone and check conversion in a month.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The change ships the same day to all users. A month later, conversion is 4.4%.
You cannot attribute this growth to the change: there is no control group, and marketing changed ad creatives that same month. The argument over whether it worked continues for another quarter.
Three other ideas remain untested. The idea from support — removing registration before the first page — was never discussed, even though it hits the very top of the funnel.
Trade-off: you moved fast, picked an idea based on who proposed it, and gained no actionable insight.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Build prototypes for all four and test with users
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: A prototype costs a day. Build four, conduct interviews, and choose what to build based on results.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
In two weeks, four prototypes and twenty interviews are ready.
The result is partially useful: you discover that people misunderstand the variant with the offer after chapter one — they think their trial has already ended. This is fixed before development at low cost.
However, the interviews do not answer the main question: all twenty people say they would subscribe, yet actual conversion is 4.1%. Stated future intent remains just words.
By the end of the quarter, no experiment has been launched.
Trade-off: you cheaply identified a comprehension issue but spent the quarter without testing a single value hypothesis.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Evaluating the first idea mentioned instead of exploring options
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Choosing an idea based on who proposed it
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Varying the entire solution instead of its independent parameters
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Hypothesis lacks a magnitude or mechanism — making it impossible to fail
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Comparing ideas only by expected benefit, ignoring the cost of inaction
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Actions for each potential outcome are not documented upfront
fields.rubric/remediation/6/gap: Sample size and duration were not calculated before launch; results are monitored on the fly
fields.rubric/remediation/7/gap: Expensive testing chosen where a prototype or feature disablement would suffice
